subject: humanities
passage: Silent films were rarely watched in silence. In the 1910s and 1920s, most theaters employed a pianist or organist, and large city theaters sometimes hired full orchestras. Because musicians often had to match music to scenes they were seeing for the first time, film studios began sending out cue sheets: lists of a film's scenes with suggested pieces and moods for each. The sheets did not dictate every note, though, and many players continued to improvise, so the same film could sound quite different from one theater to the next.
stem: According to the text, why could the same silent film sound different from one theater to another?

choices.A: Studios sent each theater its own cue sheet with different music.
choices.B: Many musicians improvised rather than playing set music note for note.
choices.C: Pianists in small theaters played louder to make up for having no orchestra.
choices.D: Cue sheets listed the exact notes each musician was expected to play.

explanation.why: The final sentence gives the cause directly: cue sheets "did not dictate every note," and "many players continued to improvise, so the same film could sound quite different from one theater to the next." The word "so" links the improvising to the differences.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text describes cue sheets for each film, not different cue sheets for different theaters.
explanation.B: Correct. The text links the differences directly to musicians' improvising.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never discusses how loudly anyone played.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the cue sheets "did not dictate every note"; they suggested pieces and moods.
